Lessons.Title: Division as an Unknown Factor
ExplanationParagraphs: Division is a missing factor in a multiplication equation: if groups × objects per group = total, then total ÷ known factor = missing factor. The result of a division equation is the quotient.

Warm-up, Notice and Wonder: original public first edition asks what pupils notice about3 × ? =12 and12 ÷3 =?. Both missing quantities are4. Use explanation rather than calling this a generic multiplication exercise.

Activity1, Equations about Onions: a farmer has14 onions equally packed into2 bags. Lin writes2×?=14, Mai writes14÷2=?. BOTH equations represent the same situation; the unknown factor and the quotient each equal7 onions per bag.

Activity2 — At the Farmers' Market: the original 2021 market picture table has FOUR rows. Row 1 Elena: 18 avocados in bags of 3; source diagram six groups of three; fill 6×3=18 and 18÷3=6 bags. Row 2 Andre: 25 tomatoes in 5 bunches; source diagram cell blank; fill 5×5=25 and 25÷5=5 per bunch; draw five groups of five. Row 3 Lin: six banana fritters equally on 2 plates; source diagram shows two groups of three; complete 2×3=6 and 6÷2=3 per plate. Row 4: no source story is printed (the situation cell is BLANK); the source draws three groups of 10, and has ?×10=30 and 30÷10=?; both missing numbers are 3. Have students propose their own story, clearly independent of source wording. Teacher reviews all four related representations.

Lesson synthesis: repeat 2×7=14 and14÷2=7 and define the result7 as quotient, showing which quantity is total, known number of bags and unknown number in each. Teacher evaluates how pupils interpret diagrams, language and partner explanations (MLR7).

The original Farmers' Market table pixels were read from the source image on the authorized Our-CS computer and all four table rows mapped; Edulytics group diagrams remain independent, not source image copies. The third-party farmers’ market photo, original student PDF and gated Boxed Muffins Cool-down were not copied or verified. Stage D, CI and academic signoff have not occurred.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: One factor is not given in a multiplication equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Related equations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplication and division can express the same equal-groups model.
KeyConcepts.Rule: a×b=c implies c÷a=b when a is not zero

WorkedExamples.Title: Number Talk related facts
WorkedExamples.Question: What are missing numbers in3×□=12 and12÷3=□?

WorkedExamples.Title: Lin and Mai's onion equations
WorkedExamples.Question: 14 onions in2 equal bags: which student is right?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain factor and quotient with group size.
Steps: Both statements refer to7 onions per bag.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both Lin and Mai;7 onions per bag.

WorkedExamples.Title: Elena's avocado bags
WorkedExamples.Question: 18 avocados in bags of three: complete the original row.
WorkedExamples.Method: Six source-drawn bags with three objects in each.
Steps: Six equal groups with three each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Andre's tomato bunches
WorkedExamples.Question: 25 tomatoes in 5 bunches: complete the original row and draw the missing model.
WorkedExamples.Method: Number of groups five is given.

WorkedExamples.Title: Lin's banana fritters
WorkedExamples.Question: 6 fritters equally on 2 plates: complete the original row.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original diagram is two groups of three.

WorkedExamples.Title: The fourth row, with a blank situation
WorkedExamples.Question: Source diagram: three groups of ten. Complete ?×10=30 and30÷10=?; invent a situation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Read source drawing and equations, then author a new context as a pupil.
Steps: The picture shows 3 groups each containing 10.
The source printed no story; a pupil must compose one.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 3 for both blanks; explanation is teacher-reviewed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say only the division equation is valid.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A missing-factor multiplication equation models equal groups too.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Match group count, size and total across both equations.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fourteen is the dividend/product, not the division result.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Give a source-provided story for the final table row.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original printed situation cell is deliberately blank.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the original three-by-ten diagram and ask students to invent their own matching situation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim 25÷5=5 only because a known product was memorized.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The blank diagram and equal-bunch context must be modelled.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw five groups containing five tomatoes; tie the factors back to the group count and size.

SummaryPoints: Lin2×?=14 and Mai14÷2=? both yield7 onions per bag.
The division result is called quotient.
Original market table four rows now read: 18÷3=6,25÷5=5,6÷2=3 and30÷10=3.
Fourth original source situation blank; learner creates it. Third-party photo/publisher Cool-down/student task PDF are not certified.
